content.title: About
content.content: Hazelnuts, also called filberts or cobnuts, are the edible seeds of the hazel tree (Corylus avellana) native to temperate regions of Europe and Asia. They have a sweet‑nutty flavor and a crunchy texture. Hazelnuts are eaten raw, roasted, or toasted and are used in baking, confections, spreads, and nut milks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hazelnuts belong to the birch family and are more closely related to oaks than to true nuts.
Sweet varieties are the ones sold for food; bitter types contain cyanogenic glycosides and are not consumed raw.
Cultivation of hazelnuts dates back over 5,000 years; the Romans prized them as a sweet treat and medicinal plant.
Hazelnuts are processed into hazelnut flour, paste (hazelnut cream), oil, and flavorings for chocolate.
Hazelnut blossoms appear early in spring before the leaves unfurl.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Hazelnuts are one of the top plant sources of vitamin E, an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Provides healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: Most of the fat in hazelnuts is monounsaturated, which can support heart health when eaten in moderation.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium in hazelnuts helps maintain normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: Hazelnuts supply plant protein and dietary fiber, contributing to satiety.

items.title: Source of copper and manganese
items.content: These trace minerals are involved in bone formation and energy metabolism.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Hazelnuts can trigger severe allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: They are calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole hazelnuts may pose a choking risk for young children.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Hazelnuts contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in prone persons.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hazelnuts can be enjoyed as a snack, added to oatmeal, yogurt, salads, baked goods, or processed into hazelnut butter and oil. Light roasting or soaking softens the skin for easier removal. Choose unsalted or lightly salted varieties.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store hazelnuts in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent oil rancidity. Discard nuts that smell bitter, sharp, or stale.
